newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-UK unions,Labour honeymoon shows strain.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-UK unions,Labour honeymoon shows strain.

text.p: The honeymoon isn't over yet but signs are that British trade unions' patience is being strained by the new Labour government's less-than-radical agenda and its continued wooing of business.
"We don't expect favours," John Monks, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), the influential body representing 74 separate unions, told Reuters in an interview.
"We do look for a change in employment law which makes the balance more fair than it is at the moment. We'll be patient but determined," he said.

The TUC, which has transformed itself into a powerful campaigning body less dependent on Labour's blessing, says its task remains to chivvy government towards a fairer deal for Britain's millions of workers.
But Monks is a pragmatist who has witnessed the unions' 18 years in the political wilderness.

He said he accepted the relationship with Labour was "evolving" and that the government had been under "enormous pressure" from special interest groups, including big business, since taking office on May 1.

"New Labour's relationship with business has been emphasised. I don't mind that but I do want to see unions have their place in the scheme of things...workers need opportunities and rights and we have made this very clear to (prime minister) Tony Blair," Monks said.
"I think workers do expect, with a Labour government in power, some improvements to their lives, there's no question about that."

Some union leaders have openly criticised Labour's modest spending plans and its "watered-down" socialism. They want Labour to grant full rights to employees from day one instead of after two years, as at present.

On its handling of the economy, Monks applauded Labour but warned that recent interest rate hikes had boosted the pound to a level harmful to industry, which would result in "considerable job losses in the autumn".
The TUC leader wants to see the pound -- now at 2.92 marks -- stabilise at around 2.50 marks.

New Labour has severed many of its links with the unions, many of which are still affiliated to the party, and moved to the centre under Tony Blair, who will address the TUC's annual conference on September 9.
The last time Labour was in power, in the strike-torn late 1970s, union bosses had a say in much of the country's industrial and economic policy.
"It isn't old Labour anymore," Monks said.

"And one of the reasons it has a majority of 179 (seats) is that it isn't. (Labour) has a broad coalition of support and we have to ensure the TUC gets a significant chunk of that support and that unions' views are taken into account."
Labour has fulfilled some of its key pledges to the unions by studying a minimum wage and signing up the European Social Chapter, a framework for employment laws.
But the TUC would like to see Blair go further and withdraw a raft of anti-union laws imposed by Margaret Thatcher's Conservative government in the 1980s.

Under Monks' leadership, the TUC has encouraged three-way partnership between government, unions and employers in a bid to engage the bosses in dialogue after the relatively free rein they enjoyed in the 1980s.

Monks said: "The TUC's relationship (with Labour) is one which is based on shared values and we're quite happy with a relationship of equality with employers. But we're not happy with one that could be termed subordinate."
Blair has already rewarded the TUC -- not itself affiliated to the Labour party -- with seats on committees overseeing the minimum wage and the crucial question of the single European currency.
Labour has also promised new legislation in the next Parliament which would give a trade union the legal right to be recognised by an employer if a majority of the company's workers wanted to belong.

"Unions tend to get publicity when there are strikes and when people are attacking the Labour party. (Union recognition) will put a tool in our hands to rebuild our base and our influence," Monks said.
